Packed red earth worn bare by generations of display, a rough circle of scrapes edged by a wall of tree-ferns three metres tall, amber afternoon light flooding the floor, the surrounding fronds trembling at the slightest footfall.

A wide river sandbar of pale amber shingle, water running fast on both sides, the far bank terraced in red clay and dark araucaria, the wet gravel gleaming under a white midday sky that fills the entire overhead.

A fern clearing twenty metres across, the canopy gap letting four hard columns of gold light fall onto deep green moss, the enclosing horsetail stems rising to shoulder height on every side, the floor spongy and yielding underfoot.

A volcanic ash flat banded in sulphur-yellow and rust-orange, shallow steam rising from three fissures along the eastern edge, the crust firm but hollow-sounding, a semicircle of dark basalt boulders on the far side making a natural backstop.

A bloom-covered meadow at full flower, magenta and deep orange to every horizon, seed-heads brushing at knee height, the whole field enclosed to the north by a low ridge of cycad palms that cuts the sky into a flat green line.

A tidal mudflat at dead low water, the cracked grey surface holding a sky of bruised violet cloud as a perfect unbroken mirror, a dense fringe of horsetails ringing the back edge, the air smelling of salt and warm sulphur.

A lakeshore of black volcanic sand, the water gone glass-still in the windless morning, a dense curtain of reeds three metres tall on three sides, a single enormous tree-fern arching over the display floor and dropping its shadow in a clean half-circle.

A rock amphitheatre, tiered sandstone benches rising in rough steps around a flat orange stage floor, iron-red streaks running vertically down the back wall, the stone hot to the touch and still radiating last night's heat into the cool dawn air.

A forest gap where a fallen araucaria sixty metres long has cleared the canopy, the enormous pale trunk itself a raised stage, the raw wound in the forest floor churned to orange clay, light falling in a single uninterrupted shaft from the gap above.

A high saddle between two ridges, cloud streaming through below in a slow white river, the ground a thin wet turf of low club-moss, the enclosing ridge-lines on both sides dark with silhouetted cycads, the air cold and bright.

A lek worn bare through countless seasons, the earth packed to the hardness of fired clay, a ring of shallow scrapes and drag-marks defining a rough circle, the surrounding tree-ferns leaning inward, one enormous drift of shed fronds piled golden in the hollow behind.

A river sandbar of cream-coloured silt, the channel braiding around both edges in shallow amber water, the far bank rising in three distinct clay terraces of orange, buff, and deep red, a single cycad standing at the apex of the tallest terrace.

A fern clearing where the ground is a carpet of unbroken bright-green moss, four columns of hard afternoon light angling in from the south-west, the clearing edged by a dense stand of giant horsetails whose ribbed stems catch the light in vertical lines.

An ash flat where the crust has banded into concentric rings of cream, pale green, and deep rust around each vent, steam rising from a long diagonal fissure, the flat surrounded on three sides by a low collar of dark welded tuff.

A meadow in full bloom, deep yellow and violet flowers to the horizon on the open side, a curved bank of low cycads closing the northern edge, the ground cover so thick and soft that each step leaves a clear pressed print for hours.

A tidal mudflat whose cracked grey surface reflects a sky of hard copper at late afternoon, a reef of dark grey mudstone running along the back edge like a natural wall, the surface firm at the centre, softening to dark wet clay near the water.

A lakeshore where cream-coloured sand meets utterly still dark water, a wall of tall reeds standing unmoved on the far margin, one massive araucaria trunk fallen half into the lake, its surface bleached silver and serving as a raised walkway to the display floor.

A sandstone amphitheatre whose tiered walls are stained deep red by iron-rich seeps, the flat floor covered in a thin skin of orange grit, one wide crack in the back wall holding a colony of small cycads that overflow down the stone like water.

A forest gap opened by two fallen giants side by side, their trunks forming parallel walls on opposite edges of a long narrow stage, the floor stripped to raw red clay by the impact, a column of bright sky visible overhead the full length of the gap.

A high saddle where the ground underfoot is deep purple-brown peat moss, both flanks dropping away into cloud, a line of wind-twisted araucaria standing along the eastern ridge like a broken comb, the cloud below lit gold by a low sun.

A lek of deep red packed earth, the display ring surrounded by a dense crescent of tree-ferns whose fronds form a continuous green canopy at four metres, a single large scrape in the centre holding a pool of rainwater the colour of strong tea.

A shingle spit of dark grey gravel curving into still water on both sides, the distant bank rising in pale horizontal layers of limestone and dark clay, the wet shingle catching the light in a thousand small glints, the air carrying the smell of green water.

A fern clearing whose floor is a solid mat of bright emerald ground-fern, the canopy gap nearly circular, the enclosing forest rising to thirty metres on every side, late light coming in at a low angle and catching the spore-haze lifting from the disturbed fronds.

A volcanic ash flat where steam vents from a long curved fissure, the crust around it banded in vivid bands of chrome-yellow, pale grey, and deep brick-red, the surrounding plain ringed by a low escarpment of dark basalt that traps the warm air close to the ground.

A bloom meadow where the flowers run from copper-orange at the edges to deep crimson at the centre, seed-heads at knee height throughout, the meadow bowl enclosed on all sides by a curving bank of tree-ferns whose fronds droop inward over the top of the display floor.
